messages.subject: Estimation with (several) random starting values
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am wondering how the nruns> 1  and  return_max=F  settings (of the mdirt function) work in mirt. As I understand it, this setting is supposed to check how often estimations starting at different (random) starting values converge to the same log likelihood value. However, mirt seems to give me only one log likelihood value.
Also, I am interested in whether those settings are applicable to the multipleGroup function.

Does anyone know how to do this?
Thanks very much!

messages.subject: How to compute EAP
messages.body_plain:
I am currently working on a research scale and we want to provide the ability for future practitioners to use this scale and produce a factorial score (latent score) when used.
To do this we want to produce an Excel sheet and programme score using VBA (just for context not usefull).
I need to transfer the calculation method to VBA, but first I want to check my calculation method on R since MIRT provide both

I want to produce 2 latent scores ML and EAP. I think I succeeded to produce ML in a Rasch model with 1 factor.
However when I compare the result are not the same and I am pretty sure I get the formulation wrong.

I used Phil Crammer's answer here to test my calculation (https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/34119/estimating-ability-using-irt-when-the-model-parameters-are-known).

So what did I miss or did worg ?

Here is my complete code.

d <- c(-2,-1,-0,1,2) # model parameter
pattern  <- c(0,1,0,1,0) # Participant response pattern

# Testing ground to produce Maximun Likeood latent score and EAP
theta <- seq(-5,5,0.0001)

# The item response function
IRF <- function(difficulty,theta){
  p <- ((exp(theta - difficulty)/ + (1 + exp(theta - difficulty))))
  return(p)
}

IRF(-2,theta) # Work fine

ML <- function(response.pattern, difficulty, theta){
  ML <- c(1)
  for(rp in 1:length(response.pattern)){
    d <- difficulty[rp]
    tmp = IRF(d,theta)^response.pattern[rp] * (1 - IRF(d,theta))^(1-response.pattern[rp])
    ML = ML * tmp
  }
  return(ML)
}

tmp = data.frame(theta,ML(pat,d,theta)) # ML work fine

# EAP not working
ml =  ML(pat,d,theta)
w <- (1/sqrt(2*3.14))*exp(-(theta^2/2))
EAP  = sum(theta*w*ml)/sum(theta*ml)
EAP

## Verification method
#generates set of random response patterns for 5 items
dat <- matrix(sample(c(0,1), 20000, TRUE), ncol=5)
colnames(dat)<-paste0('Item', 1:5)

library(mirt)
#2PL Model
sv<-mirt(dat, 1, itemtype= 'Rasch', pars = 'values')
sv$value[sv$name == 'd'] <- d*-1
#set item parameters as fixed
sv$est<-FALSE

mod<-mirt(dat, 1, pars=sv)
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE)
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE, IRTpars=TRUE)

fscores(mod,method = "ML", response.pattern = pat)
fscores(mod,method = "EAP", response.pattern = pat)

messages.subject: Re: Estimation with (several) random starting values
messages.body_plain:
You should have seen multiple log-likelihood values printed to the console to indicate the fitting of the models. mdirt() returns the value with the highest likelihood as this is most likely to be the optimal model. If you see the log-likelihoods across the models are all the same then they are all likely converging to the same location (or at least, an exchangeable one), so picking any one of them at that point is likely sufficient. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Compensatory 2PL Model
messages.body_plain:
This model is not identified, so if you were to compute the standard errors (information matrix) the model would indicate lack of convergence. For the usual model=2 exploratory IFA, the assumption is that the latent traits are uncorrelated, standardized, and that one of the factor loadings is fixed (to 0) to reach a barely identified model. This of course is arbitrary, which is why rotations are required post-estimatation. I'd suggest just sticking with the supported model constraints if your goal is to fit such an exploratory model. HTH.

Phil

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Fit statistics and Item plots in MIRT - Graded response
messages.body_plain:
While FA and IRT models have fit statistics with similar (or the exact same) names, they are different fit indices with different population values and thus should be interpreted differently. That being said, I would expect model fit information to convey similar information (e.g., your MIRT TLI is 0.43, and I would not expect your CFA TLI to be something like 0.14 or 0.94).

P
